And whatever is worth thinking over afterward—in the manner of Epimetheus—we have thought over.
Mrs Schmitt really has managed to set up a home here.
Gilles’s fish, Nay’s Leviathan, Nay’s magnificent diamond—all of them surround me again.
Like a submarine that continually reassembles itself, I make my submarine, subterranean, sublunary journey through fire and water.
Three times the Leviathan has swallowed me and then spat me out again. Now I understand the three chapters of the Book of Jonah.
Strange, by contrast, how theogonic writings are flowing toward me from every direction:
G. Nebel; the Greek gods of Fr.[iedrich] G.[eorg] J.[ünger]; Däubler’s Hymns to Italy and the Attic Sonnets.
I look out at a magnificent mountain. Behind it lies another landscape, different from the Lennetal valley where I live.
The river outside my window is splendid in winter. It looks as though it has just come into existence, without a past and without a future: pure Heraclitean present.
I am reading Troeltsch’s The Social Teachings of the Christian Churches (1912), especially this sentence (p. 173):

“The Christian theory of natural law—in which the pure natural law of humanity’s original condition, the entirely opposite relative natural law of humanity’s fallen condition, positive law which often contains the most terrible atrocities, and theocratic supreme authority, which despite all natural law claims to communicate true goodness from itself, are constantly colliding—is pitiful and confused as a scientific theory. But as a practical doctrine it is of the highest importance in the history of culture and society. It is the Church’s true cultural dogma, and as such it is at least (!) as important as the dogma of the Trinity or the other major dogmas.”
This Troeltsch would have understood me, just as I understand him. How alone I am, then!

The theological concept that truly corresponded to his political theory would have been the κατέχων, the katechon, the restraining power. Instead he wandered into this labyrinth of absolute and relative natural law!
There is a very simple sociological explanation for the hopelessness of Charles Péguy’s complaint that he could find no success among Catholics.
Perhaps the Jesuit order was the κατέχων. But what about after 1814?
Refreshing to read Hobbes on the legal position of the prisoner.
In the state of nature there are no binding agreements. These really are the elements of law.
No one else has set them out with such elementary correctness.
Power in itself is evil, says the highly cultivated Swiss gentleman.
All I can say in reply is: and powerlessness is spiteful and malicious in itself.

“The victor must not,” says Franz W. Jerusalem in the Frankfurter Hefte, December 1947, p. 1260, “rule the defeated country as occupied territory” on the pretext that the peace treaty has not yet been signed. So he still has not understood the doctrine of the discriminatory concept of war.
A just war is a bellum <infinitum>—an <infinite war>.
The doctrine of just war abolishes the <…> distinction between the enemy and the criminal.
The victor in a just war makes himself the judge of a criminal.

And depending on the scale of the crime, the judge may hang the criminal, imprison him for life, subject him to a regime of starvation and compulsory re-education, or do whatever else he considers just.
The naïveté of these jurists is unbelievable. They still refuse to see that the root of this entire problem lies in the doctrine of just war.
Like that Serene Highness speaking to the proletarians of 1848:
“But you are not allowed to do that.”
Only this time it is the <powerlessness> of the under-proletarians lecturing an all-powerful ruler about what one is allowed to do.
Am I, as a layman and non-theologian, supposed to join in discussions of Catholic questions? So that I can be instructed, as Donoso Cortés was?
Ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis.
Where you have no power, desire nothing.
I, as a jurist—that is, as a scholar already one degree removed from theology?
Flowing—the flowing of the river and of time—is Heraclitean passing-away.
Not so much becoming or coming into being as passing away.
In German, gehen, “to go,” is already contained in vergehen, “to pass away.”
To go is to go away. So the present is already the past. But nothing is said about the future. That is why Hegel’s philosophy had to become a historical view of the world.
The apparent paradox is that constant movement—that is, revolution—becomes so reactionary.
Always the same “paradox” again: the identity of opposites.
Existentialism without Christianity: that really is a performance of Hamlet without the Prince of Denmark.
Compared with that, the Marxists have a major advantage.
Tone does not merely make the music. It also makes language. Only angels sing, and only God speaks.
Since Beethoven, for us, in the beginning there is tone, no longer the Word.
(To Nette: glorification of the speaking race.)
Instrumental music solves the problem that sinful human beings should not sing, because only angels sing. Now the violins sing.
“O brave new world, That has such people in’t.”
A lovely line for New Year’s Eve 1947.
“O wonder! How many goodly creatures are there here!”

It is a touching confirmation of the year that has just ended, with a thousand threads running in every direction through an endlessly colourful fabric. It frees the words from the desperate irony of Aldous Huxley’s book title.
And yet, alas, I am being tormented by a hollow tooth: an oracle from the underworld.
On J. K. (to G. von Schmoller):

He is not a jurist but a logicist, someone devoted to pure logic, who happens to concern himself with legal problems and masters them effortlessly—schoolmasters them, in fact—because he does not suffer in the slightest from the problems that are specific to law.

Existentially, he is not a jurist. It is cheap nowadays to criticize a fashionable word like “existential.” But we should not forget what the word meant when it still had existential force of its own.
The real tests still lie ahead of us.
When they come, the foam of cleverness that has no connection with the substance of things will disappear by itself.
Of course he can do that too.
Until now, theology and jurisprudence were the “positive” sciences. They had something positively given to them: a revelation fixed in written form. Then came an enormous confusion.

Rules made by human beings for human beings were suddenly supposed to define the essence of positivism, while the supposedly assumption-free exact natural sciences claimed the word “positivism” for themselves.
Jurisprudence then shares the fate of theology. And now the abyss of the dilemma opens before it: theology or technology.
Greater sensitivity means greater hostility and an enormous increase in the possibilities of hostility.
Kierkegaard’s very real hostility toward journalists.

No one has yet thought about the infinitely sensitive instrument—the sensorium—that must arise, along with an equally intensified sensitivity to the sound of words and language, once pure instrumental music exists.
Germany overdosed on the foreign element that was, in itself, necessary.
In the end came the great vomiting, after more than a hundred years in which the demand for purity had been overstimulated beyond endurance.
You cannot return to the womb!
My present stay in Plettenberg: an arrow that has already been fired returns to the bowstring and seems to ask to be fired once again.
The somewhat naïve assumption is that the bowstring is still as tight and strong as it was fifty years ago.
Strangely, no one thinks about the archer.
Good prospects for new forms of criminalization.
Enmity will be abolished by abolishing the distinction between enemy and criminal.
Samuel Butler, Erewhon (1872), Chapter XI, “Some Erewhonian Trials”:
“Misfortune is considered more or less criminal, but it admits of classification, and a court is assigned to each of the main heads under which it can be supposed to fall.”
“It is not my business to justify the law.”
